processing: Made as black tea in BOH's highland factories; the details of each product are not usually stated by garden.
harvest_season: Little is published on seasons for this garden; highland tea in the tropics is generally picked through much of the year.
appearance_dry: Dark, fairly small leaf, as is common for commercial black tea of this kind.
appearance_liquor: Clear reddish amber, typical of highland Malaysian black tea.
taste_profile: Little is recorded about the taste of this garden on its own; expect a light-to-medium, clean highland black tea rather than a heavy lowland one.

brewing.notes: Brewed Western style. Takes milk, though a shorter steep shows the highland lightness better.

vintage_note: Sold as current production under the BOH name, without a harvest year on the pack. Most people meet it at the estate's own tea centre, so buy fresh and drink it within a year or so, as is usual for packaged black tea.
description:
Sungai Palas is BOH's showpiece tea garden in the Cameron Highlands, reached by the road up Gunung Brinchang. It is better known as a place than as a tea: the hillside rows and the tea centre with its terrace are what draw people.

The tea is ordinary in the best sense, a clean black tea from Malaysia's largest producer rather than a rare single-garden lot. Little is published on how this garden's leaf is handled separately from the rest of the company's production.

Brew it as you would any good highland black tea, with water near the boil and three minutes or so. It is a pleasant everyday cup, and it will not reward gongfu fussing.

The spelling varies between Sungai and Sungei, and both mean the same place. If you visit, drink a pot at the centre and treat the shop as a souvenir stop; for a sense of range, try the company's other highland teas next to it.
history:
BOH was founded in 1929 by J. A. Russell, whose first garden was at Habu, not here. Sungei Palas came into the company later, and the accounts differ: BOH's side is given as the 1950s, while the Malay Mail puts it in the 1960s, bought from former Danish residents.

The visitor centre and café were built in 2007 and expanded in 2019, when a new wing was named Tristan's Terrace.
